note: sha256 is of the PRISTINE upstream bytes. vendored-diff.spec.ts reconstructs them from the vendored file by stripping the provenance header block through headerSentinel plus one blank line, then inverting intendedDivergence and then deltas - last applied, first inverted. A DELTA is a mechanical rewrite forced by vendoring: an import path that cannot resolve in the flat vendor layout. An INTENDED DIVERGENCE is a deliberate behaviour change HANGAR chose (D-02), and carries the reason, the plan that chose it and a date. Both lists are inverted before hashing, so upstream's sha256 still rules: a change that is in neither list still moves the hash and still names the file. The field is written out as an empty array where there is no divergence, so a reader can tell 'none' from 'a field nobody added'.

NOTE FOR A RE-SYNCER, recorded here because it is the decision this row's arithmetic implies and does not make: the sibling touch kinds `bloom` and `disturb` carry a worse form of the same defect (residue up to 125, against comet's 1..7) and are DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE. Their repair needs a per-cell timeout derived from a per-cell start - a change to the emitted SHAPE, not to an emitted constant - and HANGAR's D-02 permission covers constants. Measured: no HANGAR preset selects either kind and touch.kind is not exposed as a knob, so neither is reachable from any catalog entry at any knob position. HANGAR's standing rule from plan 11-04 onward is that a HANGAR-owned preset must never select `bloom` or `disturb`.

When a state carries the two knot tables the module it is written to holds HANGAR's touch library (255/0 and 255/6, written by the preset landing since 12.1-08b) and the handler below emits calls into it; the simulator reads the same field to mirror the same map, so the two cannot disagree. case "perFinger": the same K as the comet's, handed the contact's closed-form hue (A-i*B, i*B, C) so the four cells take that contact's colour before they decay - K sets the colour only when handed one, and PINWHEEL's cells carry no init colouring. Same gating as the comet row (brush 1, rate 250, the naive form otherwise).

JOYSTICK 543 -> 491 at the defaults, -52 (the planner's substitution read 492 as max(raw, compressed) over one space the emitter's joiner never writes; the compiler's canonical figure is 491), knob-independent. A second contact now draws its own block where the naive one-slot glow made two fingers fight over one dot - that is the library's per-contact contract and the simulator mirrors it.

zoneStatements: with the library on the module the zone is read off the LED under the finger - local n=N(x,y), the nearest calibrated cell - and then through the LED-side zone rule ledZoneTerm (n%9*g//9 and n//9*g//9 for a 4x4 grid, //3 for 3x3, the cell itself for 9x9), the same terms the highlight and the checkerboard are drawn with, so touch and picture agree by construction at every finger position and not only at the nine LED centres; an inverted axis inverts the column or row index (8-c), never the raw value, and the snake and columns orders go through the same two terms. NINE PADS 550 -> 565 at the defaults, +15, knob-independent (the count knob moves the grid, and the shape is the same at 3x3), 343 free and still 15 under the vendored 580. The user's finding on the bench: a finger directly on the LED in row 2 column 8 lit the corner - x=120 under x*4//128 is column 3 - and a pad's outer ring took several tries.

sendsPaint's fader branch: with the library on the module the fader under the finger is N(x,y)%9*n//9 (inverted: (8-N(x,y)%9)*n//9) - the LED column the finger is on, through the LED-side rule c*n//9 the rails and blocks are drawn with - so a finger on a rail moves that fader at every position.
